title: Chapter 1 HHS Statistical Thinking
text:
Goals of Quantitative HHS Research
Most quantitative HHS research seeks to:

Describe populations and samples - descriptive purpose
Compare groups - understand differences, evaluate programs/interventions
Examine relationships among variables - how variables associate
Evaluate models with multiple predictors - what factors are most important in predicting outcomes

Researchers typically draw conclusions using statistical tests that assess:

Group differences
Correlations
Statistical significance
crumbs: 2  Chapter 1 HHS Statistical Thinking

title: Chapter 1 HHS Statistical Thinking
text:
What Is Statistical Significance?
Statistical significance addresses a simple question:

Is the observed effect large enough that it is unlikely to be zero in the population?

Examples:

Are males and females different in IQ?
Is father involvement related to girls’ self-esteem?
Is the observed correlation different from zero? Is the difference so big, it is unlikely to be zero
crumbs: 2  Chapter 1 HHS Statistical Thinking

title: Chapter 1 HHS Statistical Thinking
text:
Null Hypothesis Testing
The null hypothesis states that no effect exists
Examples:

No difference between groups
Correlation equals zero
Treatment effect equals zero

Statistical testing attempts to determine whether there is sufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis. So in your thesis/dissertation, you are hoping for p <.05 so you can “reject the null”
crumbs: 2  Chapter 1 HHS Statistical Thinking

title: Chapter 1 HHS Statistical Thinking
text:
Type I Error
A Type I error occurs when:

We reject the null hypothesis when null hypothesis is actually true

This is a false positive. We claim based on the data we collected from a sample, that an effect exists

High intensity interval training improves cardiovascular performance better than…
Spanking/physical punishment is associated with increased aggressive behaviors in children…
Smoking is related to stress…
But in the population those effects/differences don’t exist/aren’t true

The probability of committing a Type I error is determined by α (alpha), typically:

.05
.01
.001
crumbs: 2  Chapter 1 HHS Statistical Thinking

title: Chapter 1 HHS Statistical Thinking
text:
Type II Error
A Type II error occurs when:

We fail to reject the null hypothesis when a real effect actually exists

Researcher concludes that UNCG women soccer players not more likely to experience ACL tears compared to male soccer players but in reality that is true in the population…
Children in classrooms with smaller teacher-to-student ratio do not have higher reading scores…
Frequency of smoking is not associated with lung cancer…


Common causes include:

Small sample sizes
Low statistical power




Type I Type II Errors
crumbs: 2  Chapter 1 HHS Statistical Thinking

title: Chapter 1 HHS Statistical Thinking
text:
Problems with NHST
Critics argue that:

Virtually all null hypotheses are false and illogical anyway
p-values are often misinterpreted; not 95 chance the hypothesis is true
Statistical significance says little about practical importance
Lower p-values do not imply stronger effects







NoteBan on p-values?




Statistical associations offer severe critiques
Some journals attempted to ban p-values!
ASA Statement on p-values
Psych journal bans p-values (Nature, optional reading)



Researchers increasingly advocate reporting:

Effect sizes
Confidence intervals
Bayesian analyses - what is this?
crumbs: 2  Chapter 1 HHS Statistical Thinking

title: Chapter 1 HHS Statistical Thinking
text:
Statistical versus Practical Significance
A statistically significant effect may be trivial in practice
Large samples can make tiny effects statistically significant

Do I want to encourage schools to target suicide prevention to Southeast Asian students based on 8.5% self-reported suicidal thoughts among that group compared to 8.9% in other ethnic groups?

Therefore researchers should report:

Effect sizes - how big is the difference or association in standardized units
Confidence intervals - how precise or broad is the difference or association (does it come close to zero)
Practical implications - What would happen realistically if we advised policy decisions based on your results?
crumbs: 2  Chapter 1 HHS Statistical Thinking

title: Chapter 1 HHS Statistical Thinking
text:
Confidence Intervals

Confidence intervals estimate a plausible range of values for a population parameter
A parameter is a population value; a statistic is what we calculate from a sample to estimate that parameter, a better term is parameter estimate… The value we come up with that we think exists in some population
Typically we estimate something like a regression coefficient and want to assess whether that coefficient differs from zero
If we put a confidence interval around that coefficient and the interval does not include zero, that indicates statistical significance (using a p < .05 threshold)
If the interval does include zero, we cannot rule out that the true population value is zero — not statistically significant







TipRule of Thumb



A 95% confidence interval that excludes zero typically indicates statistical significance at the p < .05 level.
What a 95% CI actually means if that we somehow could do the same process of sampling participants MANY MANY times and computed a CI each time, 95% of those intervals would include the “True Population Value”
So the CI gives us a plausible range of values and tells us about the precision of our estimate as well



Visualizing Confidence Intervals


Warning: package 'ggplot2' was built under R version 4.4.3





Example confidence intervals: one significant regression coefficient (CI excludes zero), one nonsignificant regresson coefficient (CI includes zero)

title: Chapter 1 HHS Statistical Thinking
text:
APA notation

Use \(b\) for unstandardized sample regression coefficients.
Use \(\beta\) (Greek beta) for standardized sample regression coefficients.
Intercept is typically written as \(b_0\).

So in APA-style reporting, the visual distinction is:

Roman \(b\) = unstandardized coefficient
Greek \(\beta\) = standardized coefficient

section: What is the Research Question and Hypotheses
text:
What is the Research Question and Hypotheses
The Research Question and Hypotheses make a statement about how we see some human phenomenon.

RQ: Are there gender differences in suicidal thoughts?

HYP: Girls are more likely than boys to have suicidal thoughts


This hypothesis also implies a research design as this would be a comparative study with no random assignments
crumbs: 3  Chapter 2 Matching Research Designs to Analyses

objectID: Chapter 2 Matching Research Designs to Analyses.html#what-is-the-research-design
href: Chapter 2 Matching Research Designs to Analyses.html#what-is-the-research-design
title: Chapter 2 Matching Research Designs to Analyses
text:
What is the Research Design?
Is my study an experiment? A quasi-experiment? Comparing groups?

Those types of research designs tend to imply that there is a factor or categorical Independent Variable (IV) across which I expect to find a difference across groups of people

Am I considering associational or correlational relationships? Am I expecting that participants who score higher on one variable also tend to score higher on a second variable?

Are college students who report higher experiences with discrimination from peers more likely to report feelings of anxiety?
Is greater intention to exercise associated with greater numbers of steps?

This would imply an associational design with no factor/categorical variables, attribute variables (something participants “bring” with them into the study, unlike an “active” IV)
crumbs: 3  Chapter 2 Matching Research Designs to Analyses

title: Chapter 2 Matching Research Designs to Analyses
text:
How many variables are involved?

This is where analyses go from basic (Gliner et al) to complex designs
A simple comparison = a t-test
A simple association = a correlation

Those are bivariate associations

When we get more complex we will have multiple outcomes, i.e., multivariate or multiple predictors, i.e., multivariable
crumbs: 3  Chapter 2 Matching Research Designs to Analyses

title: Chapter 2 Matching Research Designs to Analyses
text:
Independent Samples t Test

Used to compare means (so continuous variables) across two groups

Examples:

Men versus women: Do women report greater parental anxiety than men?
Treatment versus control: Do participants in a smoking cessation program report less craving?
crumbs: 3  Chapter 2 Matching Research Designs to Analyses

objectID: Chapter 2 Matching Research Designs to Analyses.html#anova
href: Chapter 2 Matching Research Designs to Analyses.html#anova
title: Chapter 2 Matching Research Designs to Analyses
text:
ANOVA

Used to compare means across three or more groups

Are there differences in ethnic racial identity in college students across UNCG (a MSI), NC A&T (an HBCU), and High Point University (a PWI) ?
Is motivation to exercise higher among UNCG students who played team sports in high school compared to students who played no sports or individual sports?
crumbs: 3  Chapter 2 Matching Research Designs to Analyses

objectID: Chapter 2 Matching Research Designs to Analyses.html#ancova
href: Chapter 2 Matching Research Designs to Analyses.html#ancova
title: Chapter 2 Matching Research Designs to Analyses
text:
ANCOVA

ANOVA including covariates, or control variables

Are mean differences in depression across groups mitigated or reduced after controlling for some other factor?
In a study comparing BDNF levels in women who were clinically depressed to women who weren’t, researchers ran an ANCOVA to control for age. Results suggested lower BDNF in depressed women compared to “healthy” controls - ** the key findings ** - were statistically significant even after controlling for age. That is, the BDNF difference wasn’t due to age instead of depressed status.
In sum, ANCOVA is for situations where researchers want to draw conclusions regarding mean differences across groups while ruling out extraneous factor








Note



ANCOVA is analogous to a multiple regression when the latter has a binary predictor and additional covariates/control variables included in the model
Andy worked on a multi-site project one time where the analyst at the other site ran ANCOVAS while Andy ran multiple regressions with the intervention as the main IV and controlling for baseline. The two of us ran the same exact syntax in R…
crumbs: 3  Chapter 2 Matching Research Designs to Analyses

objectID: Chapter 2 Matching Research Designs to Analyses.html#manova
href: Chapter 2 Matching Research Designs to Analyses.html#manova
title: Chapter 2 Matching Research Designs to Analyses
text:
MANOVA
Multiple dependent variables, so a multivariate version of an ANOVA

Often employed when there are multiple outcomes of interest to compare across groups he teaching version
Example:

Are depressive symptoms, anxiety symptoms, and reports of stress higher among sexual minority youth when compared to heterosexual youth?
Rather than running multiple t-tests or three ANOVAs, can run one analysis
MANOVA accounts for the correlation among outcomes and can identify a “profile” of sorts where higher scores across groups on all outcomes are more obvious than would have been observed with multiple ANOVAs
crumbs: 3  Chapter 2 Matching Research Designs to Analyses

objectID: Chapter 2 Matching Research Designs to Analyses.html#correlations
href: Chapter 2 Matching Research Designs to Analyses.html#correlations
title: Chapter 2 Matching Research Designs to Analyses
text:
Correlations

Pearson: continuous × continuous; measures linear relationships.
Spearman’s rho: ordinal/ranked variables; nonparametric measure based on ranks.
Kendall’s Tau (τ): ordinal × ordinal; rank-based association, often preferred with small samples or many ties.
Polychoric: ordinal × ordinal; estimates the correlation between underlying continuous latent variables.
Polyserial: continuous × ordinal; estimates the correlation between a continuous variable and an underlying latent continuous variable measured ordinally.
Point-biserial: continuous × dichotomous; special case of Pearson correlation.
Phi (φ): dichotomous × dichotomous; correlation between two binary variables.
crumbs: 3  Chapter 2 Matching Research Designs to Analyses

objectID: Chapter 2 Matching Research Designs to Analyses.html#multiple-regression
href: Chapter 2 Matching Research Designs to Analyses.html#multiple-regression
title: Chapter 2 Matching Research Designs to Analyses
text:
Multiple Regression
General model:
\[Y = a + b_1X_1 + b_2X_2 + e\]
Where:

(Y) = the outcome (dependent variable) being predicted
(a) = the intercept; the predicted value of (Y) when all (X) variables equal 0
(b) = regression coefficient (slope); the expected change in (Y) for a one-unit change in (X), holding other predictors constant
(X) = predictor (independent) variable
(e) = residual (error); the difference between the observed and predicted value of (Y)

Researchers use regression to:

Predict outcomes.
Control for confounding variables.
Estimate unique predictor effects.
Test hypotheses and theoretical models.
Explain variation in an outcome ((R^2)).
Examine mediation and moderation.
crumbs: 3  Chapter 2 Matching Research Designs to Analyses

href: Chapter 2 Matching Research Designs to Analyses.html#logistic-regression
title: Chapter 2 Matching Research Designs to Analyses
text:
Logistic Regression
Used when the outcome variable is dichotomous (binary).
Examples:

Pregnant / Not Pregnant
Used Drugs / Did Not Use Drugs
Died / Survived
Passed Exam / Failed Exam

Results typically include:

Regression coefficients ((b))
Odds ratios (OR)
Confidence intervals
Predicted probabilities

Simple model:
\(\log\!\left(\dfrac{p}{1-p}\right)=a+bX\)
Where:

log(p/(1-p)): the log-odds of the outcome occurring
p: probability of the outcome occurring
a: intercept
b: regression coefficient
X: predictor variable

Interpretation:

Positive coefficients increase the odds of the outcome.
Negative coefficients decrease the odds of the outcome.
Odds ratio = exp(b).
If exp(b) > 1, odds increase; if exp(b) < 1, odds decrease.







TipCorrelation versus Regression



Key difference is that multiple regression allows for:

Multiple predictors
Statistical control
Prediction

So that movement towards greater internal validity is achieved. Does exposure to environmental toxins increase blood pressure? Does that effect remain after controlling for SES, gender, age, exercise, marital status.
Another example:
Divorce may predict adolescent depression, but that relation may weaken after controlling for inter-parental conflict

title: Chapter 2 Matching Research Designs to Analyses
section: Are ANOVAs and Regressions Really Different?
text:
Are ANOVAs and Regressions Really Different?

Many statisticians would describe ANOVA as a “special case” of Regression

That means regression is generally more flexible -

There were historical reasons why ANOVA came to be associated with experimental and agricultural research
Researchers used to think that if one was doing experiments, the appropriate analysis should be ANOVA, if doing observational/correlational research, should use regressions
I was taught that in grad school at first, then in class taught that these were all just part of the general linear model


The General Linear Model
This applies to any analysis that has a continuous (interval or ratio) or “quantitative” outcome

T-tests and ANOVAs are just a “special” case - that is, they are regressions with a categorical predictor or IV or X
If you run a t-test comparing self-esteem across boys/girls and then run a regression where you regress self-esteem on gender (dummy coded) you will get the same result!









Research question type
t / ANOVA-based approach (categorical predictor focus)
Correlation / Regression-based approach (continuous predictor focus)




Mean differences in depression by gender
Independent-samples t test (if 2 gender groups)
Linear regression with dummy-coded gender (same test as t in GLM form)


Mean differences in depression by gender, adjusting for body image
ANCOVA: DV = depression; factor = gender; covariate = body image
Multiple linear regression: depression ~ gender + body image


Mean differences in depression by gender while testing whether body image effect differs by gender
Factorial ANCOVA with interaction: gender × body image
Moderation regression: depression ~ gender + body image + gender×body image


Mean depression differences across 3+ groups (e.g., gender identity categories)
One-way ANOVA (or Welch ANOVA)
Regression with (k-1) dummy variables for group


Mean depression differences across 3+ groups, adjusting for body image
ANCOVA (multi-group)
Multiple regression with dummy-coded group + body image


Association between body image and depression
(Not an ANOVA question)
Pearson correlation (or Spearman if needed)


Predicting depression from several continuous variables (e.g., body image, stress, sleep)
(Not an ANOVA question)
Multiple linear regression


Testing combined effects of categorical and continuous predictors on depression
General linear model / AN(C)OVA framework
Multiple regression (GLM-equivalent parameterization)

title: Chapter 2 Matching Research Designs to Analyses
section: Data types, research designs, and statistics
text:
Data types, research designs, and statistics
There can be disciplinary differences in the types of data researchers used, those often map onto research design, and then those often dictate (or schould) the appropriate statistical tests that are used
crumbs: 3  Chapter 2 Matching Research Designs to Analyses

title: Chapter 2 Matching Research Designs to Analyses
text:
Data Across Academic Disciplines
Different subfields have tendencies to use particular data types. Those types vary with respect to

Sampling strategies (representative probability sampling)
Data collection strategies
Research designs

These “dictate” in a sense what analysis is appropriate
There are norms within fields, labs, etc. We will discuss how some of these are artificial in nature…



Demography
Uses large-scale, often government-collected records: Census data, vital statistics (birth/death records), and county- or state-level aggregates.

Data are typically totally numeric and secondary (collected for administrative purposes, not by the researcher).
Unit of analysis is often aggregate (county, state, tract) rather than the individual.
Designs are almost always descriptive or comparative — rarely experimental, since you cannot randomly assign counties or populations to conditions.



Human Development (Infant & Child Studies)
Because infants and young children cannot self-report, this field relies heavily on:

Observational data (you can’t ask babies questions!)
Physical/physiological measures (EEG, vagal tone, cortisol)
Informant reports (caregiver or teacher ratings) for things like behavioral ratings, social interactions

Samples are often small and frequently rely on available/convenience sampling rather than random/probability sampling. Experimental and quasi-experimental designs are possible (e.g., habituation paradigms), but much of the field is associational/correlational.






NoteExample Research Question



What factors increase the likelihood of a child having high peer sociality in first grade?




Family Studies
Data often come from observations of relational units rather than individuals alone — couples, parent-child dyads, sibling dyads, or whole-family triads.

Studies are often inherently dyadic or triadic in structure, requiring designs that account for non-independence between family members - will get into later
May incorporate genetic data (e.g., twin/adoption designs), self-reports from multiple family members, and behavioral coding of interactions
Experimental designs are possible but rare; most work is associational or comparative







NoteExample Research Questions




Are Chinese-American parents more authoritarian compared to European-American parents? (comparative)
Is marital conflict related to marital satisfaction, and does that association differ for husbands versus wives? (associational, with a potential moderator)





Public Health Studies
Draws on a wide mix of data types spanning individual and population levels:

Surveillance data (e.g., disease case reports, immunization rates)
Large cross-sectional/longitudinal surveys (e.g., BRFSS, NHANES)
Administrative/claims data
Program evaluation data from public health interventions

Data are frequently secondary and analyzed at multiple levels simultaneously (individual, neighborhood, county, state), often requiring multilevel/hierarchical models. Designs range from descriptive epidemiology, to quasi-experimental policy evaluations, to true experiments (randomized community trials) — though the latter are resource-intensive and less common.






NoteExample Research Question



Did county-level implementation of a smoke-free workplace policy reduce hospital admissions for acute myocardial infarction relative to counties without the policy?




Kinesiology Studies

Can span neuromechanics, excercise physiology, sports/exercise psychology, etc

Centers on data from physical performance and physiological measurement:

Motion capture, force plates
Heart rate / VO2 max
Muscle activation (EMG)
Wearable accelerometer data
Injury/performance records

Because many outcomes are physical and objectively measurable (not self-reported), this field is well-suited to true experimental designs (e.g., randomly assigning participants to a training protocol and measuring pre/post change) — more so than most other HHS subfields. Kinesiology also uses observational/correlational designs (e.g., comparing injury rates across sports) and quasi-experimental designs when random assignment isn’t feasible (e.g., comparing existing athletes vs. non-athletes)

Many current UNCG studies use cognitive assessment (Stroop tests), self-reports (athletic identity, exercise motivation), and can consider comparing things like self-reported versus device-informed movement/exercise







NoteExample Research Questions



Does a 12-week resistance training protocol improve gait speed in older adults more than a walking-only intervention?
Do former collegiate athletes with high athletic identity have higher levels of depression post-career?








ImportantDiscussion Questions




For each subfield above, identify one strength and one limitation of its typical data collection approach.
Why might demography rarely use experimental designs, while kinesiology more often can?
In the family studies example about marital conflict and satisfaction, why does asking “does this differ for husbands vs. wives?” turn an associational question into a moderation question?
Pick a subfield above and design a one-sentence research question that would require secondary data, and another that would require the researcher to collect primary data.

title: Chapter 2 Matching Research Designs to Analyses
text:
Levels of Measurement
The level of measurement describes how a variable is measured and determines which statistical procedures are appropriate.
As you move from nominal to ratio, each level contains all of the properties of the previous level while adding additional information.





flowchart LR

A[Nominal<br/>Categories] --> B[Ordinal<br/>Ordered Categories]
B --> C[Interval<br/>Equal Intervals]
C --> D[Ratio<br/>Equal Intervals<br/>True Zero]












NoteRemember



Each higher level includes all of the properties of the previous level.

Ratio variables are also interval.
Interval variables are also ordinal.
Ordinal variables are also nominal.




Nominal
Nominal variables place observations into categories.
Characteristics:

Categories are different from one another
There is no meaningful order
Numbers (if used) are simply labels for use in our quantitative analysis

Health & Social Science Examples

Blood type (A, B, AB, O)
College major
Therapy approach received
Marital status
Race-ethnicity
Athletic team
Gender

Appropriate Statistics

Frequencies
Percentages
Mode
Chi-square tests
If these are outcomes, nominal logistic regression (later)



Ordinal
Ordinal variables have categories that can be ranked or have some ordering to them.
Characteristics:

Categories have a meaningful order.
The distance between categories is not necessarily equal.







Tip



Andy likes the term ordered-categorical so use this from here on out…


Health & Social Science Examples

Pain rating:

None
Mild
Moderate
Severe

Agreement scale:

Strongly Disagree
Disagree
Neutral
Agree
Strongly Agree

Disease severity:

Mild
Moderate
Severe


Appropriate Statistics

Median
Percentiles
Spearman correlation — using rank orders
Mann-Whitney U — non-parametric t-test, comparison of ranks across groups
Kruskal-Wallis — like ANOVA, comparison of ranks across groups
There are ways to examine these in regressions as well — but rare







Note



Typically in the case of Likert scale items we sum these together to create a continuous variable that is more interval (next level).




Interval
Interval variables have equal distances between values.
Characteristics:

Ordered
Equal spacing
No true zero

Because zero is arbitrary, ratios are not meaningful. For example, a depression score of 40 is not twice as depressed as a score of 20.
Health & Social Science Examples

IQ score
Standardized anxiety score
Standardized depression score
T-score from a psychological assessment

Appropriate Statistics

Mean
Standard deviation
Pearson correlation
t-tests
ANOVA
Regression



Ratio
Ratio variables contain all the properties of interval variables plus a true zero, indicating the complete absence of the quantity being measured.
Characteristics:

Ordered
Equal spacing
True zero
Ratios are meaningful

For example, someone who sleeps 8 hours slept twice as long as someone who slept 4 hours.
Health & Social Science Examples

Hours of sleep
Number of doctor visits
Reaction time
Walking speed
Body weight
Daily step count

Appropriate Statistics
Nearly all common parametric analyses:

Mean
Standard deviation
Correlation
Regression
ANOVA
Factor analysis
Structural equation modeling







ImportantDiscussion Questions



When does an ordered-categorical variable “become” continuous? That might be a weird question, but think about it…
Think about the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale that is commonly used to study self-esteem.
Is it a continuous measure? If you use the scoring technique that most researchers do, then the answer is yes, because the summary score is interval level. Each of the particular items, however, are ordered-categorical

Responses are typically scored on a 4-point scale (Strongly Agree = 4, Agree = 3, Disagree = 2, Strongly Disagree = 1 for positively worded items; reversed for negatively worded items). Total scores range from 10–40, with higher scores indicating greater self-esteem.

The sum of all of these items is interval and then treated as continuous…
What if I use one item then? Or if I use techniques like Confirmatory Factor Analysis that examines individual items as outcomes? In that case, the typical analyses are incorrect… but can I never use a single item?
Often the argument is that 4 or fewer response categories implies ordered-categorical, 5 is a minimum to consider a variable continous, but 7 or more is probably better. Note that this logic has mostly been applied in the context of CFA and SEM. Also the variable should be normally distributed to be considered “continuous”

Single Likert items (1–4 categories): Treat as ordinal. Use non-parametric tests.
Single Likert items (5+ categories): Borderline; check normality assumption.
Summed/composite Likert scales (e.g., Rosenberg Self-Esteem: 10 items summed, range 10–40): Widely accepted as interval-like due to increased categories and central limit theorem approximating normality.

Practical guidance: If your data are approximately normally distributed and you have 5+ categories per item or a summed scale, parametric tests (t-test, ANOVA, Pearson r, regression) are generally robust. When in doubt, report both parametric and non-parametric results.

title: Chapter 3: Data Cleaning and Getting into R
text:
Introduction to R
R is a programming environment in which researchers can do a variety of different things. Most typically we will use R to:
1.Manage data sets 2.Clean, code data, create summary scores 3.Do statistical analyses like t-tests, regression, multilevel modeling, SEM 4.Create graphs, tables, and figures
But R can do a number of other tasks for us like reading OSF pages, scraping internet sties, renaming files, and converting files to PDFs.
Why R?

It is Free!
It is open-source which means that anyone can access, add to R and its numerous packages
It uses a simple programming language developed by experts, you can see all source code (unlike some proprietary stats packages)
This all means that there are new additions to R all the time to keep up with state-of-the-art changes in statistics


Who will enjoy R the most?

People who like programming!
People who enjoy learning new code, exploring what R can do
Those looking to streamline work time by using convenience features related to creating tables in APA style

Benefits of learning all that R can do for academic researchers

Saves time and energy when creating reports
Fewer mistakes transcribing output to tables and figures
Can access anywhere (unlike networked software)

Makes it faster to analyze data
All analyses we want to do are possible with R

section: What steps do you take to get started?
text:
What steps do you take to get started?
Download R from https://cran.r-project.org/
Download RStudio from https://posit.co/downloads
Find videos, tutorials, free books on GitHub, AIs are pretty good with R code

What is the difference between R and RStudio?
R is the programming language in which we write code and execute commands. RStudio is a GUI (graphical user interface) that simplifies many of the basic tasks (e.g, reading in an SPSS file, installing packages, viewing plots) that we typically want to accomplish with R.
RStudio is what we will predominantly use in class and there are four sub-windows in R Studio:

Console for running code immediately
Script editor for saving code or running chunks of code
Environment pane showing objects you’ve created
Files/Plots/Help pane for outputs and documentation

Beyond the advantage of being able to more easily do basic tasks than with R, RStudio also has syntax highlighting, code suggestion/completion, spellcheck, and some smart coding routines

Warning



## What Are Outliers?
An outlier is an observation that is unusually distant from the bulk of the data — either extremely high, extremely low, or both (in multivariate settings). Outliers may reflect:

Data entry errors (e.g., age coded as 999)
Measurement error (e.g., equipment malfunction)
True but rare observations (e.g., a legitimately high income in a low-income sample)
Violations of study protocol (e.g., participant who didn’t follow instructions)


How to Detect Outliers
Univariate (single variable): -

Visual: Boxplot, histogram, scatterplot — look for points far from the main cluster
IQR method: Mark as outlier if value < Q1 − 1.5×IQR or > Q3 + 1.5×IQR -
Z-score method: Mark as outlier if |z| > 3 (more conservative: |z| > 2.5) -
Range checks: Compare to known valid ranges (e.g., age should be 0–120)

Multivariate (multiple variables):

Mahalanobis distance: Measures how far a case is from the centroid of all variables combined
Cook’s distance: Identifies cases with high influence on regression coefficients
Leverage + residuals: Cases with high leverage and large residuals are flagged




R Code Example:

library(dplyr)

Attaching package: 'dplyr'

# IQR method
df <- tibble(age = c(25, 30, 28, 32, 999, 27, 29))  # 999 is an outlier

Q1 <- quantile(df$age, 0.25)
Q3 <- quantile(df$age, 0.75)
IQR <- Q3 - Q1
lower_bound <- Q1 - 1.5 * IQR
upper_bound <- Q3 + 1.5 * IQR

outliers <- df %>%
  filter(age < lower_bound | age > upper_bound)

# Z-score method
df <- df %>%
  mutate(
    z_age = scale(age)[, 1],
    is_outlier = abs(z_age) > 3
  )

:::: ::: ## Coding Categorical Variables

Nominal: no inherent order (e.g., race/ethnicity, program site, referral source).
Ordered categorical: ordered categories without equal spacing assumed (e.g., Likert items, severity stages: mild/moderate/severe).
Dummy coding: reference group = 0, comparison groups = 1; coefficients interpreted relative to the reference.
Effect coding: groups coded -1/1; coefficients interpreted relative to the grand mean.
Note that we will get into coding specifics in R when we run analyses… ::: ::: callout-warning ## Common Pitfall

Numeric-looking codes (1 = Male, 2 = Female) get accidentally treated as continuous in R if not explicitly converted to a factor — this silently corrupts downstream models. Also, there are many good reasons for why binary variables should be recoded to 0/1. For example, got divorced = 1, did not get divorced = 0 as opposed to 1 and 2.

Easier interpretation of intercepts in regressions
Easier interpretation when doing product terms for interactions
Mean is actually meaningful (will be percentage of participants in 1 category) ::: ::::

ImportantDiscussion Questions



We need to be really careful with nominal IVs. Say for example I want to see if there is greater participation in blood pressure screening at Urban Health Clinics, Rural Clinics, or via TeleHealth visits (using home BP monitor)
I would most likely have a variable titled “Clinic Type” that has values of 1, 2, and 3 that represent Urban, Rural, and Telehealth, respectively

section: What is an ANOVA? Why would you do one?
text:
What is an ANOVA? Why would you do one?
ANOVAs are an analysis that is typically done to compare means across 3 or more groups.
Let’s take for example a comparison of Hmong American adolescents who were classified into three groups based on their experiences as cultural and language brokers.






Note



Hmong are a refugee group originally from the mountain regions of Laos who were drawn into the Vietnam conflict by US forces. Upon US withdrawal from SE Asia, many Hmong fled persecution and violence and were placed in refugee camps in Thailand. Many were granted refugee status to come to the US. There are an estimated 400,000 Hmong in the USA with the largest populations in California, Minnesota, Wisconsin, and North Carolina.
Cultural and language brokering refers to children in immigrant families serving as translators/interpreters for non-English speaking parents and also teaching parents about social rules and norms in the US.

(vang2019a?)


In a survey of 7th grade adolescents, I asked students about experiences as cultural and language brokers. Based on those responses, I classified students into one of three groups: (1) Low, (2) Moderate, and (3) High. The classification reflected adolescents who reported very low engagement in cultural/language brokering or just doings things like answering the phone. Moderate engagement was some frequency of doing translating, particularly at school. High engagement referred to adolescents who frequently translated for parents including in “high stakes” settings like medical appointments.
My research questions included:

Do Hmong adolescents who engage in high levels of cultural and language brokering differ from adolescents who are lower in cultural and language brokering?
In terms of self-esteem, conflict with parents, and GPA

One main hypothesis I had was:

Hmong adolescents who engage in high levels of cultural and language brokering will report higher mean levels of culture-related conflicts with parents compared to adolescents who engage in moderate and low engagement.

From the perspective of an ANOVA, the null hypothesis would be: \[H_0: \mu_{low} = \mu_{moderate} = \mu_{high}\] Where \(\mu\) refers to group means
An appropriate statistical test to evaluate this hypothesis would be an ANOVA because of the comparison of means across three groups. The specific details of ANOVAs, computing \(F\) statistics, and other technical points come later. Here we are focused on the conceptual aspect of what ANOVA is testing, how to run the ANOVA, and its interpretation.
The central test statistic in ANOVA is the \(F\) statistic. Just like when we do a \(t\)-test, there is a critical values associated with \(F\) that is determined by the chosen significance level (\(\alpha\), often .05) and the model degrees of freedom (\(df\)). Unlike a \(t\)-test, however, the \(F\)-distribution requires two sets of degrees of freedom: one for the numerator (between-groups variation) and one for the denominator (within-groups variation).
The \(F\) statistic is computed from the sample data. If the obtained \(F\) statistic exceeds the critical value, or equivalently if the \(p\)-value is less than \(\alpha\), the researcher rejects the null hypothesis and concludes that there is a statistically significant difference among the population means. Specifically, the conclusion is that at least one group mean differs from at least one other group mean, although the ANOVA itself does not indicate which groups differ. Follow-up analyses, such as posthoc tests, are needed to determine the specific group differences.
A common follow up test is the \(Tukey\) Honestly Difference test that will do group-by-group posthoc tests to identify specific statstically significant differences across the three groups (as in our case).
Typically it is also helpful to see the means stratified by group and to compute a measure of effect size, \(\eta^2\) or \(\omega^2\).

Using R to run the ANOVA
The three AAFCS means are 24.27, 29.57, and 28.41 for the Low, Moderate, and High groups respectively.






NoteSample Write up



A one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was conducted to examine differences in AAFCS scores across participants with low, moderate, and high levels of cultural brokering. There was a statistically significant F(2, 77) = 3.51, p = .035, η² = .084 indicating mean differences in AAFCS scores across groups. Group means indicated that participants in the moderate brokering group (M = 29.57) reported the highest AAFCS scores, followed by the high brokering group (M = 28.41) and the low brokering group (M = 24.27).
Posthoc tests (Tukey’s HSD) suggested that the moderate brokering group scored significantly higher than the low brokering group (mean difference = 5.30, 95% CI [0.04, 10.56], p = .048). The differences between the high and low brokering groups (mean difference = 4.14, p = .143) and between the high and moderate brokering groups (mean difference = -1.16, p = .884) were not statistically significant.

text:
Technical Details about ANOVAs

Why can’t we just stick with \(t-tests\)?
For the above study, I might have thought about doing \(t-tests\). For example, couldn’t I have just done one \(t-test\) comparing the LOW group to the moderate group, then another \(t-test\) comparing the LOW to the HIGH group and another to test moderate versus HIGH?
While that is possible, there is a statistical problem that occurs when running multiple tests. When running multiple tests, researchers run the risk of creating Type I Error Inflation. What that means is that multiple tests increase the risk of committing Type I errors (rejecting a null that really is true, i.e., claiming a significant difference that is not really different).
Think about the various different research questions we might have related to group comparisons: Is motivation to exercise different across adults who played different types of sports? Are reports of anxiety different across different sexual orientation and gender identity groups?
These questions involve tests of more than two groups and doing multiple \(t-tests\) would raise lead to alpha inflation and raise the familywise error rate.






NoteFamily wise Error Rate (FWE)



When we think of Type I errors, we think about a specific test. For example, what is the probability of us making a Type I error when doing a \(t_test\) to evaluate if males have higher self-esteem than females. This is a per-comparison error rate
When we conduct multiple statistical tests, such as a series of pairwise \(t_test\)s across several groups or outcomes, those tests form a family of tests. The probability of making at least one Type I error across that entire set of tests is called the familywise error rate (FWE).
FWE refers to the probability of incorrectly rejecting at least one true null hypothesis when multiple statistical tests are conducted. In general, as the number of statistical tests increases, the likelihood of obtaining a statistically significant result purely by chance also increases.
Consequently, the FWE becomes larger than the target significance level (e.g., α = .05) used for any individual test.
The formula to compute the increase in the FWE is \(\alpha_{FWE} = 1 - (1 - \alpha)^K\)
If doing 3 comparisons:
\(H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2 = \mu_3\)
\(\alpha_{fw} = 1 - (.95)(.95)(.95) = 1 - .95^3 = 1 - .8574 = .1426\)
This suggests that, if all null hypotheses are true and the three tests are independent, there is about a 14.3% chance of obtaining at least one statistically significant result by chance alone.
Put differently, even when there are no real group differences, running three separate tests at (= .05) makes it more likely that random sampling variation will make one of them appear statistically significant.








Note



Note that the above procedure assumes independent tests.
A different approach is the Bonferroni bound:
[ _{FW} (.05) = .15 ]
This means that if we conduct three tests, each at (= .05), the probability of making at least one Type I error is no greater than (15%).
The () symbol is important. Unlike the calculation
[ 1 - .95^3 = .1426, ]
the Bonferroni bound does not assume that the tests are independent. It works even when the tests are related or share data, as pairwise comparisons among group means often do.
Because it gives an upper limit rather than an exact probability, it may be somewhat conservative. In this example, the actual family-wise error rate could be below (15%), but Bonferroni guarantees that it will not exceed (15%).
When running multiple tests, The Bonferroni correction is a simple way to keep the overall probability of one or more false positives at or below a chosen family-wise significance level.
The rule is:
[ _{} = ]
If we want the family-wise error rate to stay at (.05) and we have three comparisons:
[ _{} = = .0167 ]
Therefore, instead of using (p < .05) for each comparison, we use:
[ p < .0167 ]
A comparison must have a (p)-value below (.0167) to be statistically significant after the Bonferroni correction.

Important tradeoff
The Bonferroni correction reduces false positives, but it also makes it harder to find real effects.
In other words:

It lowers the chance of a Type I error (false positive).
It can increase the chance of a Type II error (missing a real difference).

For a small number of planned comparisons, such as three, Bonferroni is easy to use and often reasonable. For many comparisons, it may be too strict, and other methods—such as the Holm correction or Tukey’s HSD—may be better choices.





ANOVA overcomes the alpha inflation problem by focusing on one test.

The \(F\) test is an omnibus test of whether there are mean differences across multiple levels of a factor

That one test controls FWE rates and reduces risk of Type I error
The test only suggests that mean differences exist in two at least one pair of group means
Often follow-up tests are needed to sort out specific differences across groups or levels of factors

title: Chapter 4 ANOVAs Part I
text:
One Way ANOVA details
Addresses mean difference questions across multiple groups.

Conceptually ANOVAs are extensions of \(t_test\)s

Doing an ANOVA with two groups would be the same as a \(t_test\)

ANOVAs are multiple group, non-directional tests
Use one Type I error rate

The technical statistical test asks:

Are the observed group differences larger than would be expected due to random variation?

Instead of comparing two means directly, ANOVA compares:

Between-group variability to within-group variability

So while our goal is to compare means, the Analysis of Variance includes evaluations of variances as a means to test for group differences.

The Logic of ANOVA
If groups truly differ:

Group means should be far apart and individuals within groups should be relatively similar


library(ggplot2)

# The group means are held constant in both panels.
# Only the within-group standard deviation changes.
group_means <- c(
  "Group 1" = 0,
  "Group 2" = 0.50,
  "Group 3" = 1.00
)

scenarios <- data.frame(
  scenario = c(
    "Large within-group variation\n(smaller F ratio)",
    "Small within-group variation\n(larger F ratio)"
  ),
  sd = c(1.15, 0.35)
)

# Create normal-distribution curves for each group in each scenario.
plot_data <- expand.grid(
  x = seq(-3.5, 4.5, length.out = 500),
  group = names(group_means),
  scenario = scenarios$scenario,
  KEEP.OUT.ATTRS = FALSE,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

plot_data$mean <- unname(group_means[plot_data$group])
plot_data$sd <- scenarios$sd[
  match(plot_data$scenario, scenarios$scenario)
]
plot_data$density <- dnorm(
  plot_data$x,
  mean = plot_data$mean,
  sd = plot_data$sd
)

# Data used to draw a dashed line at each group mean.
mean_lines <- expand.grid(
  group = names(group_means),
  scenario = scenarios$scenario,
  KEEP.OUT.ATTRS = FALSE,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
mean_lines$mean <- unname(group_means[mean_lines$group])

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = x, y = density, fill = group, color = group)) +
  geom_area(alpha = 0.28, linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_vline(
    data = mean_lines,
    aes(xintercept = mean, color = group),
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 0.8,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~scenario, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Group 1" = "#3B82B9",
      "Group 2" = "#E68613",
      "Group 3" = "#35A853"
    )
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Group 1" = "#3B82B9",
      "Group 2" = "#E68613",
      "Group 3" = "#35A853"
    )
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-3.5, 4.5), ylim = c(0, 2.0)) +
  labs(
    title = "The ANOVA F Ratio: Differences Between Groups Relative to Differences Within Groups",
    subtitle = "Dashed lines represent group means. The means are the same in both panels.",
    x = "Outcome score",
    y = "Relative frequency",
    fill = "Group"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "gray35"),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )







Figure 5.1: ANOVA compares variability between group means with variability within groups. The group means are identical in both panels; only within-group variability changes.











Note



Take this back to a \(t_test\) for a moment. The \(t_test\) formula is a ratio of mean differences over variability within groups.
\[t =
\frac{\bar X_1-\bar X_2}
{
\sqrt{
s_p^2
\left(
\frac{1}{n_1}+\frac{1}{n_2}
\right)
}}\]
The resulting t-ratio is conceptually a ratio of between group differences (in means; the numerator) to within group variation. What this formula basically is saying is that the difference between two groups (variation between groups) is evaluated by standard errors that capture within group differences (how different participants in each group are; within group differences)


ANOVA evaluates:
\[F =
\frac{
\text{Between-Group Variance}
}{
\text{Within-Group Variance}
}\]

text:
Understanding the F Ratio
Let’s think about what this means: The ANOVA is creating a ratio of between group variance to within group variance

The between group variance is going to capture differences in the means across groups - i.e., how the means vary or differ across/between groups
The within group variance is going to capture differences in scores within groups, or how different people in the same group are from each other
A bigger F essentially means that groups differences are relatively large relative to within group differences


Computing the F Ratio
To compute the F Ratio, we would need to compute the between group variation and the within group variation, then compute that ratio.The resulting ratio can be thought of an index of separation between the groups.
Technically the F Ratio is computed by dividing the Mean Sum of Squares for the between group variation \(MS_B\) and the Mean Sum of Squares for the within-group variation \(MS_W\).
The hand calculation involves computing each of these two values, then creating the ratio.

The first step in manually computing an ANOVA F Statistic is to compute the Mean Squares of the Between group variance
Quick reminder the variance of a set of scores is computed by summing deviations from a mean
\[s^2 = \frac{\sum (X_i - \bar{X})^2}{n - 1}\] The variance for group American-Oriented Group would be the sum of squared deviations, divided by the sample size (minus 1). We would take each score, subtract the group mean, square that value, then sum that number, then divide by 9.
The analogous formula for the Between-Group Variance (\(MS_B\)) = \(SS_B/df\)
\(SS_B/df\) is computed as an extension of the variance for a sample (above). The differences between each group mean j and the grand mean squared are multiplied by the group sizes \(N_j\) and then summed to get the \(SS_B\). The degrees of freedom are the number of groups \(K - 1\).
\[SS_B = \sum_{j=1}^{K} N_j (\bar{X}_j - \bar{X})^2\]
\[df = K-1\]
Which leads to:
\[MS_B = \frac{SS_B}{df}\]
In addition to computing the \(MS_B\) we also compute the \(SS_W\)
That means that the \(F\) statistic is comparing/computing two sources of variance: Between group variance and within group variance.






Note



The Between Groups SS is just the deviations of each group mean from the grand mean squared, then summed, and multiplied by the number of values in each group. That value is then divided by the between groups \(df\) which is \(K\)-1 (or # of groups, minus 1).
In our case since these groups are equal, then \(N_1\) = \(N_2\) = \(N_3\) = 10
The mean of the groups are:
\(\bar{Low}\) = 26.40 \(\bar{moderate}\) = 29.60 \(\bar{High}\) = 32.50 and the grand mean = (26.40+29.60+32.50)/3 = 29.50


The computation for \(SS_B\) then would be

mean_low<-26.40
mean_med<-29.60
mean_hi <-32.50

grand_mean<-29.50

group_size_low<- 10
group_size_med<- 10
group_size_hi <- 10

SS_B <- ((mean_low-grand_mean)^2)*10 + ((mean_med-grand_mean)^2)*10 + 
  ((mean_hi-grand_mean)^2)*10

# Then the MS_B is calculated as SS_B/K-1 or

MS_B <- SS_B/2

MS_B

The computation of the \(SS_W\) is a bit more complicated in that this captures within group variance and necessitates subtracting each individual score from the group mean.
The group means are 26.40, 29.60, and 32.50 for the Low, Moderate, and High brokering groups, respectively. Individual participant’s scores within each group are deviated from those means, then squared, then summed. Those values capture within group variance.
\[ SS_W = \sum_{j=1}^{K}\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}(X_{ij}-\bar{X}_{j})^2 \]
\[X_ij\] = The i or individual score in group j (low, moderate, high)
\[\bar{X}_j\] = The group mean, e.g., the low group mean of 26.40
So each deviation in a group squared, then summed together, then summed across the groups

# Create group means in the data
# Aggregate command sorts, sort scores in aafcs by brok_three, using toy_brokering
# note "toy" is just a term for a practice dataset
# aggregate using means

group_means <- aggregate(aafcs ~ brok_three, data = toy_brokering, mean)

# Add the means back into the data using "merge"
# merge the group_means back in as a variable, sort by the brok_three
# so each participant in a group gets the group mean as their score
# suffixes just gives the name to the variable

toy_brokering <- merge(toy_brokering, group_means, by = "brok_three",
            suffixes = c("", "_mean"))

# Squared deviations from group mean
# Create an object call deviations
# that is going to be scores for each participants' aafcs score
# subtracting out their group mean scores - deviated from a group mean
# then those values are squared to get the squared deviations

toy_brokering$deviations<- (toy_brokering$aafcs - toy_brokering$aafcs_mean)^2

# Sum them up to get the total SS_W

SS_W <- sum(toy_brokering$deviations)

Large values of F indicate that between-group variability is much larger than within-group variability, suggesting that at least one group mean differs from the others.
The null hypothesis is \[H_0 = \mu_1 = \mu_2 = \mu_3\]
where \(mu\) is each group mean.
The \(F\) is evaluated for statistical significance if the test statistic we just computed is more extreme than the critical value for \(F\) at our chosen p value and the model number of degrees of freedom.
